logline: A modern woman is swept back to 10th-century Goryeo during a solar eclipse and becomes entangled in deadly royal succession politics, falling for the battle-scarred fourth prince despised by the court.

renewal.note: Single season of 20 episodes, concluded November 1, 2016 on SBS. Adapted from the Chinese novel Bu Bu Jing Xin by Tong Hua; a standalone conclusion with no Korean continuation announced.

bollymeter.basis: IMDb 8.6 reflects strong international fan devotion; domestic reception was more muted at a 7.6% Nielsen average, with critics citing pacing damage from a 20-episode compression of source material designed for 35 episodes.

seasons.review_body: Moon Lovers: Scarlet Heart Ryeo aired on SBS from August to November 2016 with a US$13 million budget and an ensemble headlined by Lee Joon-gi, IU, and Kang Ha-neul. It performed commercially below expectations in South Korea, averaging 7.6% on Nielsen Korea. Internationally, the drama gained notable traction, becoming the first Korean series to trend on Tumblr globally and building a devoted following on Chinese streaming platforms. The story itself falls into two distinct halves: the first leans into court intrigue, ensemble chemistry, and Lee Joon-gi's brooding performance, while the second compresses the narrative as network editing trims roughly half the source material's plot into the remaining episodes. The result is a great story visibly constrained by pacing and episode-count limits, though the emotional core continues to land for committed viewers.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 1
episode_reviews.review_body: Moon Lovers: Scarlet Heart Ryeo Season 1 Episode 1 aired August 29, 2016 on SBS as the premiere of a 20-episode historical fantasy that averaged 7.6 percent on Nielsen Korea domestically while becoming the first Korean series to trend on Tumblr globally. IMDb audiences scored the series 8.6, reflecting strong international fan devotion that outstripped the domestic reception. The premiere deploys its time-travel premise efficiently: a modern woman, a solar eclipse, and a sudden arrival in Goryeo's royal court within the first act. The large ensemble of princes is introduced with enough visual differentiation to be navigable. Lee Joon-gi and IU establish the show's central dynamic in their first shared scene, and the $13 million budget is visible in the period production design.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The premiere deploys the time-travel conceit with brisk efficiency - a modern woman, a solar eclipse, and a sudden arrival in Goryeo's royal court. The opening also introduces the drama's aesthetic: lush period costumes, a large ensemble of princes, and immediate romantic and political complication.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The solar eclipse sequence that transports the female lead into Goryeo, establishing the show's premise in one visually striking scene.

episode_reviews.title: Episode 20
episode_reviews.review_body: Moon Lovers: Scarlet Heart Ryeo Season 1 Episode 20 aired November 1, 2016 on SBS as the series finale of a 20-episode historical romance that averaged 7.6 percent on Nielsen Korea. IMDb audiences scored the series 8.6, with the international following on Tumblr and Chinese streaming platforms constituting the show's primary fanbase. The finale delivered the tragedy the show had been building toward. Critics who flagged the compressed pacing of the final episodes noted that the source material's 35-episode arc had been condensed to 20, and the resulting loss of narrative space is most visible in the finale's final stretch. The separation sequence became the most-cited moment in the show's legacy as one of K-drama's best-loved tragic romances.
episode_reviews.spoiler_free: The finale delivered the tragedy the show had been building toward - a conclusion that satisfied viewers who valued melodrama and frustrated those expecting a genre concession toward reunion. The compressed pacing of the final episodes remained a point of criticism even among the show's admirers.
episode_reviews.the_moment: The separation sequence that defines the show's legacy as one of K-drama's best-loved tragic romances.
